newsitem.title: CHINA: China opens war memorial hall, vows to be strong.
newsitem.headline: China opens war memorial hall, vows to be strong.

text.p: Top Chinese officials on Monday opened a new wing of a memorial hall marking Japan's invasion exactly 60 years ago and vowed that a richer, stronger China would never again fall prey to outside bullying.

Vice-chairman of the powerful Central Military Commission Liu Huaqing and propaganda chief Ding Guan'gen presided over the opening of the Memorial Hall for the Chinese People's War of Resistance Against Japan near Beijing's Marco Polo Bridge.

"Although 60 years have passed, we will never forget the heinous crimes of burning, killing, raping and looting committed by the Japanese imperialists on Chinese soil," Beijing city's Communist Party chief Wei Jianxing said at the opening ceremony for the hall's new wing.

The ancient Marco Polo Bridge in the southwest of the capital was the site of a July 7, 1937, clash between Japanese and Chinese forces that sparked Japan's full-scale invasion of China, in which Beijing says 35 million Chinese died.

Authorities poured in 70 million yuan ($8.4 million) to build the new wing of the memorial hall, increasing floor space by 30,000 square metres and adding more than 6,000 photographs to highlight Japan's wartime atrocities.

Beijing has been eager to publicise events marking its war of resistance against Japanese aggression as a way to boost patriotic sentiment among its huge population and to remind Tokyo of its militaristic past.

Officials also jumped at the chance to use the event to stir up support for supreme ruler Jiang Zemin in his role as heir to late paramount leader Deng Xiaoping's economic reforms, which have turned China into a regional economic and military power.
"The Japanese dared to invade us at that time because our economy was backward, the country was weak, and the people were poor," Wei said.
"Today, we must use a fierce sense of national mission and responsibility to build the motherland into a strong, rich and democratic socialist modern society," Wei said.

On Sunday, China called for greater vigilance against resurgent Japanese right-wing forces, slamming would-be militarists for trying to whitewash Tokyo's World War Two history of aggression against China.
Revisionist politicians have portrayed Japan's military expansion in the 1930s as liberating Asian neighbours from Western colonial rule instead of aggression.
"Japanese rightists still absolve themselves and refuse to admit to the cruel crimes of invasion," Wei said.

Ageing revolutionaries, groups of soldiers and busloads of schoolchildren toured the new hall, recently declared by the ruling Communist Party to be one of 100 "demonstration bases" to educate the masses and stir up their patriotic sentiment.
"This memorial hall will be good for today's Chinese people, especially the young, so that we won't forget this national shame," said Zhou Lingluo, a Beijing government worker.
Sober-faced visitors toured the exhibits, many expressing outrage at the more gruesome displays such as one of Japanese doctors performing a surgical experiment on a Chinese victim.
"This is so horrible," said one Navy seaman. "How could they do such things?"
Others said while they and future generations should not forget the suffering brought by the war, there was much ground for new friendship between the Chinese and Japanese peoples.
"The past is in the past, now is now," said one 83-year-old woman surnamed Song.
